notes: This catalog slice fills the gap between low-power professional GPUs and very-high-capacity local AI accelerators using current NVIDIA RTX PRO Blackwell workstation products.
Hardware specifications come from NVIDIA product pages/datasheets. Canadian prices are point-in-time retailer observations and are not treated as MSRP.
NVIDIA AI TOPS are vendor peak FP4 figures with sparsity and are not directly comparable with AMD/Intel TOPS or measured LLM tokens/s.
Model-fit guidance is approximate because runtime overhead, KV cache, context length, quantization and framework memory behavior materially affect capacity.

hardware.form_factor: 2.7 in H x 6.6 in L, dual-slot low-profile
hardware.model_size_practicality: Best suited to 7B-14B class quantized models and smaller high-context workloads. 16GB is the hard capacity limiter despite strong software support.
hardware.quantization_compatibility: Broad CUDA support for GGUF and common weight-only INT8/INT4/FP8/FP4-capable inference paths; actual low-precision kernel availability depends on runtime and model.
hardware.llm_inference_suitability: Strong compact always-on CUDA option where 16GB is sufficient. Memory bandwidth is modest, but the 70W envelope and mature software stack are unusually practical.
hardware.performance_per_watt_note: 288 GB/s at 70W is about 4.11 GB/s of memory bandwidth per watt.
hardware.cost_efficiency_note: Current Canadian pricing is much higher than 16GB consumer cards, but this buys ECC GDDR7, workstation drivers, low-profile packaging and 70W operation.
hardware.off_grid_suitability: high for a CUDA discrete GPU; 70W board power makes it comparatively solar/battery friendly.

pricing.note: PNY RTX PRO 2000 Blackwell 16GB listing; retailer pricing and stock are dynamic.

hardware.form_factor: 4.4 in H x 10.5 in L, dual-slot full-height
hardware.model_size_practicality: Excellent single-card tier for 14B-30B class quantized models and large-context smaller models. Some larger 4-bit models can fit depending on runtime overhead.
hardware.quantization_compatibility: Broad CUDA support including common GGUF/INT8/INT4 paths; Blackwell adds FP4-capable Tensor Cores where frameworks expose suitable kernels.
hardware.llm_inference_suitability: Strong balance of 32GB capacity, 896GB/s bandwidth, 200W power and mature CUDA integration.
hardware.performance_per_watt_note: 896 GB/s at 200W is 4.48 GB/s per watt.
hardware.cost_efficiency_note: Acquisition cost is premium relative to 32GB gaming or AMD workstation cards; value is primarily CUDA maturity, ECC and professional form factor.
hardware.off_grid_suitability: medium; 200W is substantial but materially easier to sustain than 300-600W high-capacity cards.

pricing.note: Dell add-in card listing; other Canadian retailers were observed around CA$4,740-5,000.

hardware.form_factor: 4.4 in H x 10.5 in L, dual-slot full-height
hardware.model_size_practicality: 72GB is a particularly useful single-GPU capacity tier for 70B-class 4-bit weights with careful runtime/context budgeting, and comfortably handles 30B-class models with large KV caches.
hardware.quantization_compatibility: Excellent CUDA support across FP16/BF16, FP8 and common INT8/INT4/GGUF workflows; FP4 acceleration depends on Blackwell-aware kernels and compatible model formats.
hardware.llm_inference_suitability: One of the strongest single-card local-LLM workstation options below 96GB because it combines 72GB capacity, 1.344TB/s bandwidth, active cooling and mainstream CUDA.
hardware.performance_per_watt_note: 1,344 GB/s at 300W is 4.48 GB/s per watt.
hardware.cost_efficiency_note: Very expensive in Canada, but it avoids multi-GPU partitioning for many 70B-class quantized workloads and provides more usable capacity than 48GB professional cards.
hardware.off_grid_suitability: low-medium; 300W is demanding but still half the power of a full RTX PRO 6000 workstation card.

pricing.note: PNY RTX PRO 5000 72GB Blackwell listing; price and stock are dynamic.

hardware.product: RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Max-Q Workstation Edition
hardware.form_factor: 4.4 in H x 10.5 in L, dual-slot full-height
hardware.multi_gpu_positioning: NVIDIA explicitly positions Max-Q for dense workstation configurations up to four GPUs.
hardware.model_size_practicality: 96GB single-GPU capacity is large enough for many 70B-class quantized deployments with substantial context headroom and can host some larger weight-only quantizations depending on runtime overhead.
hardware.quantization_compatibility: Broad CUDA support for FP16/BF16/FP8 and common INT8/INT4/GGUF workflows; Blackwell FP4 acceleration requires compatible kernels/model formats.
hardware.llm_inference_suitability: Exceptional single-GPU local inference capacity with 1.792TB/s bandwidth. The Max-Q variant is unusually attractive because it retains the same memory capacity and bandwidth as the 600W Workstation Edition at a 300W board limit.
hardware.performance_per_watt_note: 1,792 GB/s at 300W is about 5.97 GB/s per watt, roughly double the memory-bandwidth-per-watt of the 600W Workstation Edition using the same 1,792GB/s memory subsystem.
hardware.cost_efficiency_note: Extremely high purchase price, but technically superior to the full 600W Workstation Edition when throughput-per-watt and dense multi-GPU deployment matter more than maximum single-card compute clocks.
hardware.off_grid_suitability: medium-low in absolute terms, but unusually strong for 96GB dedicated VRAM; 300W is far easier to power than the 600W full Workstation Edition.

pricing.note: NVIDIA-branded Max-Q listing observed at CA$16,899.99; PNY listings were around CA$17,999.99 and Dell higher.
